Alteration of DAMPs after TBI leads to multi-organ pathological and systemic changes

Alteration of DAMPs after TBI leads to multi-organ pathological and systemic changes. The primary injury in TBI leads to the overproduction of DAMPs. This excessive release of DAMPs triggers an inflammatory response that is detrimental to brain cells. The activation of microglia and astrocytes, alongside neuronal injury, further exacerbates secondary brain injury, manifesting as oxidative stress, cell death, excitotoxicity, BBB dysfunction, brain edema, and neuroinflammation. During the early stages of secondary brain injury, the immune response in the brain predominates; however, the peripheral immune response subsequently influences the entire body. The HPA axis and ANS may affect the immune response following TBI. On one hand, neurohormones weaken innate immunity and increase the risk of bacterial or aseptic infections in patients with TBI. On the other hand, extracellular vesicles (EVs) carrying DAMPs released by nerve cells can be distributed through various bodily fluids, including blood, lymph, and urine, leading to systemic pathological changes. Pulmonary complications are often among the most serious and frequent consequences of TBI. Respiratory failure associated with ALI has a notably high mortality rate. NPE exacerbates dyspnea in patients with TBI, potentially linked to the MAPK–NFκB inflammatory pathway triggered by S100B and HMGB1 in the lungs; changes in liver function following TBI are characterized by increased SAA1. As hepatocytes are the primary source of SAA1, its elevation serves as a damage marker in patients with TBI. Furthermore, within 12–24 h post-TBI, increased liver enzyme activity (ALT and AST) reflects hepatic injury. Numerous experimental and clinical studies indicate that, during acute and chronic hepatitis, the expression of HMGB1 and IL-33, along with that of their receptors RAGE and ST2, respectively, is significantly upregulated. It can be speculated that, in the long-term pathological phase of secondary brain injury, the onset and progression of hepatitis are related to the transport of DAMPs from the CNS to the entire body via EVs after TBI; TBI also impacts kidney function, where elevated renal load following systemic vasoconstriction may heighten the risk of AKI. Impaired kidney function could disrupt fluid balance within the body, exacerbating cerebral edema and increasing the risk of systemic edema. Kidney diseases that are closely associated with the overexpression of multiple HSP subtypes, including HSP70, HSP90, and HSP27, include chronic glomerulonephritis, ischemic and toxic AKI, and obstructive nephropathy. EVs laden with DAMPs can circulate throughout the body via various fluids, underscoring the close relationship between post-TBI renal functional changes and DAMP transport; the heart is subject to numerous cardiovascular abnormalities, including ECG changes, arrhythmias, and the release of cardiac injury biomarkers. Severely affected patients with TBI may exhibit LVD, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, NSM, and abnormal heart rates, indicating persistent autonomic dysfunction. The binding of HMGB1 to TLR4 on cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells is a significant contributor to hypertension following TBI; gastrointestinal function after TBI is primarily characterized by mucosal damage and intestinal flora imbalance. The inflammatory factors and chemokines released into the gastrointestinal tract due to heightened neuroinflammation are critical causes of mucosal damage. The imbalance of intestinal flora is also influenced by the ANS, hindering the digestion and absorption processes in patients with TBI, prolonging disease duration, and negatively impacting prognosis. Consequently, TBI involves multi-organ damage throughout the body via the HPA axis, ANS, and immune system. Importantly, DAMPs within the brain can be transported to various organs via EVs, which play a crucial role in this process.
